name: Swarnapureeswarar Temple, Semponarkoil
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Sambandar and Appar
period: Tevaram era; renovated under Aditya Chola I, later inscriptions
summary: Semponarkoil, near Mayiladuthurai, honours Shiva as Swarnapureeswarar — the golden-hued lord — whose self-manifested form is said to have sparkled like gold. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by Sambandar and Appar, the place is rich in divine legend: it is remembered as Lakshmipuri, where Mahalakshmi did penance; as Indirapuri, where Indra won the vajra; and as the shrine where Dakshayani worshipped the lord before Daksha's sacrifice. Its very name, Tiruchemponpalli, speaks of fine gold.

sections.history: Semponarkoil, also called Tiruchemponpalli, is an ancient Shaiva village near Mayiladuthurai, hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and Appar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. The temple's art and inscriptions carry its history: an image of Jyeshta Devi in a niche points to renovation in the time of Aditya Chola I, while inscriptions record the reigns of Kulothunga Chola III, Rajadhiraja I and, much later, Serfoji of Thanjavur — a span of patronage across many centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Swarnapureeswarar, a self-manifested lingam said to have shone like gold. Chola-period sculpture, including the Jyeshta Devi image that helps date the renovation, and inscriptions on its walls make the temple a record in stone of successive dynasties. The several sacred names of the place — Lakshmipuri, Indirapuri, Kandapuri — are each tied to a divine worshipper remembered here.
sections.legends: Many gods are said to have worshipped at Semponarkoil. Mahalakshmi did penance to Shiva here to win Vishnu as her lord, so the place was called Lakshmipuri. Indra worshipped the lord to obtain the vajra with which to slay the demon Vruddhasura, giving the name Indirapuri; and Murugan worshipped here before destroying Tharakasura, giving Kandapuri. The temple is also remembered as the place where Dakshayani, Shiva's consort, worshipped him before going, uninvited and against his wish, to her father Daksha's sacrifice. The golden sheen of the self-manifested lingam gives the lord the name Swarnapureeswarar.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam. The temple's many divine associations — with Lakshmi, Indra, Murugan and Dakshayani — lend their own colour to its observances, and the proximity to the great temple centres around Mayiladuthurai draws pilgrims on the wider delta circuit.
sections.experience: Semponarkoil rewards the pilgrim with a temple whose every name tells of a god who came to worship here, and whose golden lord is set in finely carved Chola stone. The darshan of Swarnapureeswarar, amid inscriptions and sculpture spanning many reigns, gives the visit the depth of a place long cherished across the ages.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Semponarkoil is near Mayiladuthurai (and Sembanarkoil town) in the Nagapattinam/Mayiladuthurai delta, roughly 15 km from Mayiladuthurai; the nearest rail heads are Mayiladuthurai and Sirkazhi, with local buses and taxis to the temple.
